question.text:
You are a portfolio manager provided with the expected return and standard deviation of four assets. Asset A: Expected Mean Return: 5%, Standard Deviation: 0; Asset B: Expected Mean Return: 10%, Standard Deviation: 10%; Asset C: Expected Mean Return: 12%, Standard Deviation: 15%; Asset D: Expected Mean Return: 7%, Standard Deviation: 17%.
Assume the risk-free rate is 0%. Which of the three risky assets (B, C, or D) has the highest Sharpe Ratio?

explanation.text: The Logic: Sharpe Ratio = (Expected Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Standard Deviation. With the stem's stated Rf = 0%: Asset B = (10 - 0)/10 = 1.00; Asset C = (12 - 0)/15 = 0.80; Asset D = (7 - 0)/17 = 0.41. Asset B delivers the highest risk-adjusted return. Sources: NISM-Series-XXI-A workbook pp.148-149 (Sharpe formula) and p.157 (Rf as required input). The Trap: Picking C feels natural because 12% is the top absolute return, and "B & C" tempts candidates who think high-return plus moderate-risk must tie. The trap is confusing absolute return with risk-adjusted return — Sharpe explicitly penalises every unit of standard deviation. In the audit-flagged original, the risk-free rate was not stated; under any unstated Rf above ~6% the ranking would change, so the keyed answer was only correct under an unstated assumption. Note: The original stem omitted the risk-free rate that the Sharpe formula on p.148 requires. The stem has been tightened to state Rf = 0% explicitly (matching the worked-example pattern on p.157, where Rf is always an input), making Asset B the uniquely highest-Sharpe risky asset.
